title: how a shell-mediated file read reaches the nudge and the capture worklist
summary: One table in hooks/evidence.mjs decides what counts as reading a file, and it deliberately gives two different answers to two consumers: the PostToolUse nudge asks only whether content was put in front of the agent (bashContentRead), while the capture worklist asks which NAMED file was read (the tier attached to each path token). The same command can therefore clear the grep-spiral nudge while anchoring no note at all — `python3 -c 'print(open(sys.argv[1]).read())' src/cli.ts` is a real read with no literal path to attribute. Both surfaces reach that one table by three different host routes, so a fix applied to Claude's path alone leaves Codex and Cursor silently broken.

steps.role: the single classification table: read verbs, inline-script file-open APIs, and per-token tier
Claude PostToolUse consumer — asks INTENT only, via bashContentRead
Codex consumer, a verbatim twin of the Claude handler
Cursor consumer — delegates to the Codex handler through adaptCursorInput, so it inherits fixes without its own patch
renames Cursor's Shell tool to Bash so the shared detectors match unchanged
pins all three hosts x both surfaces, because a one-host fix fails silently

invariants: `cat` must never go back into SEARCH_RE in either nudge handler — it prints a whole file, which is a Read by another name
hooks/nudge-handler.mjs and hooks/codex-nudge-handler.mjs are verbatim twins apart from their header comment; patch both in the same change
inline scripts are classified BEFORE the segment split — the splitter cuts on `;`/`|` that are the script's own syntax, not shell operators
the read tier attaches only to the path named inside the read call; other path tokens in the same command stay mentions
